title_en: Journey to Malwa and Separation from the Guru
translation:
Thereafter, on the tenth day of the bright half of Ashwin in Samvat 1687 — Vijaya Dashami — Vaishnav Gopaldasji and Vaishnav Jivandasji set out together from Choranda for Malwa (a region of Madhya Pradesh near Bhopal). In Malwa, Gopaldasji had a fellow devotee, a friend. They arrived at his temple, his home. He showed them great respect. Vaishnav Jivanji cooked the meal, and they took the offering — guru and disciple, Gopaldasji and Jivanji Maharaj, eating together. That night they held satsang (holy company), and unbroken hari-kirtan (devotional hymn-singing) took place. When they thought of staying a second day, the devotee said to his wife that between them they would not be able to provide meals for both guests. Vaishnav Jivandasji overheard this. Then Gopaldasji too gave his consent: "Jivan, you go on to Ujjain; I shall stay here." No sooner had this been decided than midday arrived. Jivandasji pressed to set out at once, so the woman of the house brought a plate of shyam bhoji.

(From the behaviour of this friend's wife it appears that Gopaldasji's fellow devotee in Malwa, too, must have held the same lofty outlook as our own Uda devotees — for even though she could not feed two visiting guests, she still lovingly served Jivanji Maharaj a plate of shyam bhoji as he departed. "Shyam bhoji" is the elevated term our Uda devotees adopted for boiled toor dal, ordinarily called bakra.)

In the world people call boiled toor-dal grains "bakra" and regard it as a poor, coarse food fit for people of low, base station — hence the saying "even a ghost is pleased with bakra," meaning a person of low caste is pleased even by such a trifling meal. But our community of devotees holds to the same love-devotion as Lord Krishna, and so, just as the simple folk of Vraj were delighted with a bakra-like food for their midday snack — the very food Shri Krishna himself used to eat — we address it by the sacred name "shyam bhoji." Not only that, but in Puniyad in earlier times only the offering of shyam bhoji was served; no khichdi or any other dish was cooked. That offering of shyam bhoji continued in Puniyad down to recent times, and to eat it the devotees would lovingly make plates from banyan leaves gathered in the courtyard — until once a devotee fell from the banyan tree, after which the revered Lakshmiba began preparing khichdi instead. Even so, from this incident of the Malwa woman's offering of shyam bhoji, one can see what an influence the mighty guru Gopaldasji must have had even upon his fellow devotees.

Loving devotees fondly called shyam bhoji by the name "jalpan" (light refreshment). Taking this offering, they got ready to leave. Then Jivandasji said to Gopaldasji: "O Gopaldasji! When we set out from Gujarat, you asked whether devotees of Vishnu should not keep maya (worldly wealth) at all." That is, when the journey began from Choranda, Jivandasji had said they should carry some money with them, and Gopaldasji had replied that Vaishnav devotees have no need of maya, since he had many friends in Malwa where they could stay comfortably. But now separation had come to stand between guru and disciple. At this Jivanji Maharaj said: "Had we kept maya, the two of us could have stayed together and worshipped the Lord together; this separation that has befallen us is the doing of maya. So maya, too, has its place in the devotion of Vishnu." Saying this, he recited a sakhi (couplet).

_Maya hamari atma, deh kriyake kaj. Parmatma hamare Jivana, Sitapati Bijraj. ||1||_ (Maya — wealth — is extremely necessary for the upkeep of our body, but our highest goal, the true bent of our mind, we shall keep fixed on devotion to Sitapati Ram and to Krishna, the king of Vraj.)

_Maya sathe Jivana, milkar kije bat. Harijankun Hari melve, aurankun lagave lat. ||2||_ (One should deal with maya, O Jivan, thoughtfully and with understanding, for it can even help Hari's devotees attain God. But those who fall into infatuation with wealth are kicked away by it and cast into the cycle of birth and death.)

_Kabir maya mohani, mange mile na hath. Manse utari jab hi, tab dolan lagi sath. ||3||_ (Kabir says: maya is enchanting; even striving to obtain it, it does not come into our hands. But the moment we turn our mind away from it, it starts walking along beside us, pleading.)

_Kabir maya dakani, sab kahun kun khaye. Dant upadu papani, jo santa nedi jaye. ||4||_ (Kabir says: maya is a witch-demoness who kills and devours everyone. But if she goes near the saints, Kabir will strike her so hard that her wicked teeth are torn out.)

_Kabir kar jodi maya khadi, thadhi det asis. Bilsi aur latan chhadi, samar samar Jagdish. ||5||_ (Kabir says: maya now stands with joined hands, giving blessings — she has abandoned her wanton ways and her kicking, and stands remembering the Lord of the world again and again.)

Kabirji speaks another sakhi of this same sentiment: _Kabir bhoot pret aru dakani, chetak aru jamkal, jo harijan dware avahi, tab Harji kadhe khal. ||1||_ (Ghost, spirit, witch, black magic, and the messenger of death — should any of these come to a devotee's door, Hari himself strips off its skin.)

Here again comes up, once more, the very matter Jivanji Maharaj had raised at the start of the Samagam: that for a devotee of Vishnu, maya is a great veil cast over Brahma, and the whole universe is covered by that veil — so how, then, does the soul cross over? The very question on which this scripture was composed appears again here. This is an extremely difficult and knotty question, and along with it "maya" is the obstacle. Yet here it is precisely the absence of maya that has brought separation between guru and disciple — so its true cause is maya itself. Both of them were free of worldly desire; both had set out for the spread of devotion and for meeting with saints. Jivanji Maharaj further says that had they kept maya (wealth) with them, the two of them could have stayed together and carried on their devotional work; but since separation has now come between them, the question arises: what is this "maya"? What is its true nature?

Various schools of philosophy and various commentators have viewed and evaluated the word "maya" in different ways. The first world-teacher, Adi Shankaracharya, called maya "mithya" (illusory). Declaring "Brahma is real, the world is illusory," he held that the world — all things moving and unmoving that can be seen, heard, or experienced, this whole world perceptible to the senses — is itself "maya," and is unreal.

Here "maya" has been used in two senses: (1) maya as wealth, property, riches, money; and (2) maya as desire, craving, and attachment toward the material — in short, one sense is spiritual and the other material. Even so, maya remains a wondrous thing.

Looking at the views of other commentators on Vedanta philosophy: Shankaracharya describes maya as the unknown, the unreal. Bhaskaracharya calls it ignorance without actual substance. Ramanujacharya, Shrikhand, Nimbarkacharya, and Shekhar all view it in the sense of "wondrous." Madhvacharya holds it to be the mind's affliction of the soul, brought about through the Supreme's primal power. Vishesha Bhikshu calls it divine power. Vallabhacharya calls it the power, the influence, of the Supreme Lord. Pandit Aryamuni calls it the power of knowledge.

In the Vedas, maya-avidya is used in the sense of "error" or "delusion." In the Isha Upanishad it is said that truth is covered by a golden vessel — hiranyamaya (a kind of white cloth, like madharpat, once worn in ancient times; Omkara too is of this nature, for it stands before Brahma like a veil of white cloth) — this covering is called Brahma, and in the Samagam, Om itself has been called a golden vessel. In the Katha Upanishad, darkness is spoken of: the blind lead the blind; take refuge in knowledge and ignorance departs; this ignorance-darkness is called maya. Jivanji Maharaj has spoken of this "blind pursuit."

_Ram Krishna je Jivana, do sagun avatar. Andh dhandh kaha bhaju, je Ved na pave par. ||2||_ (Prabodh) (Ram and Krishna, O Jivan, are the two manifest incarnations of God. So why keep chasing some blind pursuit — holding the false delusion of being unable to grasp whether God is formless and attributeless, or what he truly is — instead of simply worshipping Ram and Krishna? Even Brahma himself could not settle that question.)

_Andh dhandh vede tajyo, aaye Jamna kool. Jahan Brahma sanatan Jivana, Ramkrishna nij mool. ||3||_ (Prabodh) (Having tired of saying "not this, not this" — that God is neither with attributes nor without — Brahma gave up all such efforts and came to the bank of the Yamuna, to Krishna; for it is there, O Jivan, in Ram and Krishna, that the eternal Brahma truly, originally abides.)

The Mundaka Upanishad calls the very "knot of ignorance" itself maya. The Brahmakaranya says, "asato ma sadgamaya, tamaso ma jyotirgamaya" (lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light) — meaning the unreal, or tamas (darkness), is itself maya. The Rigveda uses it in the sense of "appearance," abhas.

The Shvetashvatara Upanishad calls it Prakriti (Nature), and calls the wielder of maya "Maheshwar." Other Upanishads use it in the sense of "mithya" (unreal). Later, maya also came to be understood as the Vaishnavi "leela" (divine play). Ramanujacharya also gives "maya" the meaning "wondrous."

In the Atma Purana: (1) that which does not occur in any of the three times — past, present, future; (2) that which is the cause of the world in its causal form; (3) that which veils the true self-nature of all beings; (4) that which is destroyed by right knowledge.

In the Padma Purana: "ma" means Lakshmi, or else it means liberation. Thus maya herself has fallen into the web of maya — in the present age maya, as Lakshmi, has drawn the world to her, and it is she who is worshipped there.

In truth maya and Brahma are not separate, but since the Vedantins regard Brahma alone as real, the various Vedas and Upanishads have given differing definitions of it. The revered Yadunath Maharaj, comparing the outlooks of the jnanis (men of knowledge) and the saints, observed that the difference between them is as vast as that between sky and netherworld. He writes that, set beside the explanatory style of the philosophical schools — through the great Vedic sayings such as "Prajnanam Brahma," and statements like (1) Tattvamasi, (2) Ayamatma Brahma, (3) Aham Brahmasmi, and so on — the style of the saints is altogether distinctive. Showing the difference between the devotee and God, Adhyaruji says in Vadu Ghol:

_Avigat dev anant niranjan, bhavbhay bhanjan Shri Vasudev. Jag ghade bhaje jeh, nav lahe kon per teh._ (God is unmanifest, endless, and stainless, the destroyer of worldly fear, Shri Vasudev; it is he who fashions and dissolves the world, and no one can grasp in what manner he does so.)

This is the nature and function of God — creation and destruction are God's own work. Then, showing the work of the devotee, it is said: _bhav narak tale bhakt_ (the devotee wards off the fear of the world and the hell that follows from the sin born of one's own wrongdoing); freeing others from fear is itself the devotees' vow. Merely by the sight of saints, all three kinds of affliction are removed — just as approaching a fire removes cold at once, needing no further proof. Baba Kabir shows the sequence of steps for attaining Brahma, and through it the greatness of saints becomes apparent as well.

This, then, is the style of the scriptures and of the saints. Sadguru Baba Kabir has set out below the sequence for reaching the state of Brahma, and it must be reflected on and practised repeatedly — anushilan meaning to study the very same thing again and again. To instil fear in others is the work of wicked people. _Manushyanam sahastreshu kaschidyatati siddhaye_ (among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection). Among these, the style of the Gita is celebrated the world over, yet the style of the saints is distinctive from it. The revered Yadunath Maharaj has put this beautifully: the devotee joins with maya and strives to attain God, and yet is not entangled by it. This much concerns the tradition of the acharyas; let us now look at it according to the tradition of the saints.

Gyaniji Maharaj calls maya "kanak-kamini" (gold and woman). Kuba Bhagat says "maya dindash jasi" — maya is nothing but a passing, momentary impulse. Kabirji calls it ego, ahankar; he calls maya the black serpent-queen, the serpent being a symbol of ego. Vedanta calls knowledge Brahma, but for devotees knowledge is not what matters — knowledge brings ego, and that is a sign of downfall, so devotees do not accept mere knowledge.

Besides these, saints such as Narsinh Mehta, Mirabai, Tukaram, Pipaji, Rohidas, and Surdas have described worldly attachment and infatuation itself as maya. Saints live in the world and yet perform bhakti (devotion); maya does not hinder them, because no infatuation or attachment to the world remains in them — they remain like the lotus leaf on water, engaged only in devotion. There is a difference between the devotee's maya and the world's maya; whoever understands this difference can conquer the world — for one man turns a palace into a wilderness in his mind, while another builds a palace in the wilderness. Let us look at the words King Janak once uttered in ancient times.

_Anantamiva me vittam yasya me nasti kinchichan, Mithilayam pradiptayam na me dahyati kinchan. ||1||_ (Mahabharat, Shanti Parva 178-2) (Janak says: though I possess boundless wealth and splendour, none of it is truly mine; if Mithilapuri were to catch fire, nothing of mine would burn — for whatever burns, I have no attachment to it.)

This is the true greatness: whoever lives detached never comes to grief. But here a real predicament falls upon guru and disciple, and no way out can be found. Whatever remedy exists is only a way of letting the time pass. Here even the principles and reasoning of the scriptures prove false, for reality speaks otherwise — a scripture that seemed reasonable to the mind yesterday breeds only confusion today. No one truly accepts maya, and yet today maya is showing its full power: separation has fallen between guru and disciple. Kabirji has said — whom has this maya not troubled? It troubled Indra, Narad, at every turn even Shiva, and Kans, Shishupal, Gorakhnath; it has troubled even the greatest of warriors — only poor Kabirji alone has it not troubled.

A dialogue took place between Kapil and Syumarashmi. Caught in the confusion of maya's bondage of action, Syumarashmi asks Kapil Muni thus: _Naiva tyagi na santushto nashoki na niramayah, na nirvidhitso navritto napavritto'sti kaschan. ||2||_ (Mahabharat, Shanti Parva 269-46) (In truth, in this world no one is wholly a renunciant, nor wholly content; no one is free of grief, nor free of disease; no one is wholly without the desire to act, nor wholly free of attachment, nor wholly a renouncer of action.)

That is: even one who outwardly renounces wealth and splendour, in truth attains all comfort and splendour in some other form, and suffers no real hardship. Thus even such a "renunciant" is, in reality, neither happy nor content, and his craving and indulgence go on increasing day by day; he can neither carry out his tasks fully nor withdraw from them completely. (Here "karma" does not mean ritual acts, sacrifices, and the like, but simply the work one must do to live one's life.) Thus man is in every way sorrowful and afflicted. What, then, is the release from his sorrow? How is one to become free from suffering?

At the very beginning of this Samagam, Jivanji Maharaj himself asked: how does the soul cross over? In answer, he answers this question for us step by step throughout: even a sannyasi is not happy, even a renunciant-yogi is not happy. But here the answer is given for how one may become happy while living in the world — namely, without becoming wholly attached to it, and without turning away from the Supreme Brahma. That is why it is said: maya is necessary for our livelihood; we shall live amid it, mixing with it, and yet we shall not be blinded by infatuation with it, and shall continue to follow the Supreme Brahma — this indeed is the devotee's task. Kabirji, for his livelihood, kept weaving cloth his whole life long. Pipaji, though a king enjoying boundless splendour, kept himself turned away from the desire for pleasure even while managing his kingdom's affairs, and still advanced on the path to attaining the Supreme Brahma. Narsinh Mehta never once cared about his own poverty, and yet he attained not merely happiness but the very rank of a supreme devotee — his life is like an open book.

This incident at Malwa is, for Jivanji Maharaj, merely the first chapter of the book of life's struggle. Here we are given direct, living proof of exactly what his aged guru wished to demonstrate. It is from here that Jivanji Maharaj's true life-journey truly begins. The four years of rest at Choranda had been only a battle of words, a study of books; but today its living, tangible experience stands directly before him. Man's real test lies precisely in this: it is only when reality comes and stands directly before him that his patience is truly tested. Today both of them are distraught. Jivanji Maharaj has been placed in a state of utter helplessness — one cannot simply leave one's aged guru and go on alone, and yet there is no other way. Jivanji Maharaj sought permission with just a glance, and Gopaldasji watched him leaving; he could say nothing. He understood that this was their last meeting — that he would never again meet his beloved disciple. Thus separation came between the two.

The following day the Malwa devotee gave Gopaldasji leave to move on as well, and so, setting out from there, he too went on to Ujjain. It was in Gopaldasji's mind that he would meet Jivanji there — Jivanji Maharaj had said, on leaving, that they would meet at Ujjain. Bidding a final "Ram Ram" to Vaishnav Gopaldas, Jivanji Maharaj had gone on ahead. Gopaldasji, in separation from Jivanji Maharaj, departed for his heavenly abode on the fourth day at Ujjain. Thus, after parting at Malwa, he stayed four days at Ujjain and then went to his own heavenly abode. Even today there stands in Ujjain a Gopal temple; it is possible that it was at this very spot that Gopaldasji left his body, though we have no certain information of this.

Having taken leave of Gopaldasji, Jivanji Maharaj walked through the forest for four days and nights. On the fourth day, overcome with hunger, he sat beneath a behedaa (myrobalan) tree and ate its fruit. After eating it, he lay unconscious beneath that tree for a full day and night, with no awareness of his body at all.

In the world, fear and superstition have grown enormously. Great scholars, instead of dispelling such superstition, have gone on increasing it among the timid and weak — it would not be wrong to call such scholars fools. Consider: for women we accept that there is such a thing as ritual impurity during menses, but what can we say of those who ascribe this same fault of impurity even to water, earth, and trees? Such scholars have planted in people's minds the superstition that if you sit under a behedaa tree, you will end up in hell (Bhagavati Katha, part 40, page 7).

Ayurveda, in fact, makes very good use of behedaa in medicine, and there is a saying that beheda, hirda, and amla together make triphala churna. The kernel of the behedaa fruit is poisonous, but its bark is useful; behedaa causes constipation and induces sleep. It is likely, then, that Jivanji Maharaj, distressed by famine, ate behedaa fruit, and that this is why he remained unconscious for four days. In tantra practice there is a rite in which one goes naked under a particular constellation, brings back sticks of behedaa wood, fashions a peg from that wood, recites a banishing mantra, and drives it into the ground at a place — whereupon the residents of that place flee, and the place is left desolate.

In the Atharvaveda, in the "Abhichara Kalpasutra," the details of such abhichara (black-magic) rites are recorded. Harmful tantric rites of sacrifice mention six kinds of abhichara: marana (killing), mohana (bewitching), stambhana (paralysing), vidveshana (causing enmity), uchchatana (banishing), and vashikarana (subjugating). Those who perform these abhichara rites are held to be punishable. (Registration no. 448, page 984.)

Jivanji Maharaj was not one to be frightened by superstition and fear, and he did not wish to look upon the behedaa tree with contempt. Compelled by the helplessness of the famine, he must have had to eat the kernels of the behedaa fruit — those kernels are tasty, and eating too many of them must have brought on his intoxicated, unconscious state.

On his return journey, after some days, he arrived at Jagannath. There he had the direct darshan of Lord Jagannath, and stayed there for several days. During this stay, one evening at dusk, Vaishnav Jivandasji was sitting leaning against a pillar when he entered a state of bhava-samadhi (devotional trance), and no outward consciousness remained in him. As night fell, the temple priests closed the doors and went away, and Jivanji Maharaj was left behind inside the temple. It is said that no one is permitted to stay overnight inside this temple — folk belief holds that anyone who spends the night in the temple either comes out dead in the morning or goes mad. Even today, for this reason, no one is allowed to spend the night there.

All the temple attendants closed the doors and left; Jivanji Maharaj remained inside. At midnight, an endless resounding began — endless instruments playing and singing was heard. Jivanji Maharaj heard this sound directly, and yet no one was to be seen; no one had entered the temple, nor was anyone outside, and yet the sound went on. (A more detailed account of this incident is given in Jivandasji's Parchari, composed by Shyamdasji — see Uda Dharma Panchratnamala, page 241.)

In this temple, Ekadashi is said to be hung upside down, and so no fast is observed there on the day of Ekadashi. Moreover, people of all eighteen varnas eat together there, seated in a single row.

Thus the night passed, and in the morning, when the attendants opened the doors, they saw Jivanji Maharaj seated inside in bhava-samadhi. They were struck with great astonishment — for no one is supposed to be able to remain inside — and when they saw this rare and exceptional saintly man seated in the temple in devotional trance, everyone bowed with devotion at his feet.

Thus, after staying here some time, Jivanji Maharaj came to Ayodhya seven days later. There he had darshan of the ancient Ayodhya. It is said, according to the view of the Puranas, that this is the place where King Ram ruled for eleven thousand years — that is, after Ram departed for his heavenly abode, Ram-rajya continued for eleven thousand years, meaning the kingdom went on being governed according to Ram's own righteous principle. The extent of this Ayodhya was sixteen yojanas (a yojana being an old measure equal to about four gaus, or eight miles, roughly thirteen kilometres — by this reckoning the kingdom's extent would come to about two hundred and eight square kilometres). When Raghunathji (Ram) departed for his heavenly abode, all the inhabitants of Ayodhya prepared to go along with him. Maharshi Valmiki writes:

_Tatah sarva prakritayo Ramam vachanamabruvan, gacchantam anugacchamo yatra Ram gamishyasi. ||3||_ (Ramayan, Uttarkand 107-12) (Then all the people said to Ram: "O Ram! Wherever you go, we shall all follow you there.")

The Adhyatma Ramayan, in the ninth chapter of the Uttarkand, verse 66, also says: _Tato vimagra sarayujaleshu nara parityajya manushyadeham, aruhya divyabharana vimanam prapushcha te santanikakhyalokan. ||4||_ (As soon as all those people plunged into the Sarayu and gave up their human bodies, they at once received divinely adorned bodies and a celestial chariot, and, seated in that chariot, went to the realm called Santanik.)

Besides human beings, God also took with him the souls born in tiryak yoni, the animal kingdom. "Tiryak" refers to living creatures other than humans — animals, birds, and the like — for when such a creature stands up, its head does not rise straight up as a human's does but stays horizontal, and its food, too, does not travel straight down into the stomach but goes in sideways; hence "tiryak" carries the meaning "crooked, horizontal."

Seeing the love of all the townsfolk, Ram gave everyone leave to come along with him. Of this it is said: _Brahmadikanam sannidhye sanathikritya devatah, brahmalokadhva chandala asheshaprani sanhitah. ||30||_ (In the presence of Brahma and the other gods, having brought the deities under his protection, Lord Ramchandra took with him to heaven every being, from the outcaste to the Brahmin, and all the Gandharvas — and so Ayodhya became a wilderness.)

That is, on going to Vaikuntha, knowing the heart's wish of all his people, he took with him every inhabitant of Ayodhya, from the poorest outcaste to the wealthiest, and all the animals, birds, and insects; all who bathed together with him in the Sarayu went along to Vaikuntha.

_Svanitah sarvagandharvastenayodhya vanikrita, Ramenoktau sutau satyarajyartha salakshmanih. ||31||_ (All the Gandharvas were led away with him, and by this Ayodhya was turned to forest; Ram, together with Lakshman, instructed his two sons Lav and Kush to rule the kingdom righteously.)

In this verse, in place of the words "tenayodhya vanikrita," there is a variant reading "chira-ayodhya"; hence the commentary within the Samagam explains it as "Chira Jodhya van keta-i." "Chira Jodhya" means the old Ayodhya, and the word "ketai-van" is a corruption of "kantar-van." "Kantar-van" means a forest of kovidar trees, or else a great, dense, uninhabited forest; "kantar" can also mean sugarcane or bamboo. One might say that trees like the kovidar must have grown up in the old, desolate Ayodhya. Further, if we take the sense of "ketai," it may also be a corruption of "kataka," meaning the kataka fruit — that is, nirmali — the powder of which, when put into dirty water, makes the water clear. So it may be said that the animals, birds, and other creatures of the tiryak yoni who dwelt in Ram's Ayodhya, by the power of Ramchandra's glance, gave up their bodies as they plunged into the water and went along with Ram. Thus Ram made Ayodhya like a nirmali-kataka fruit that cleanses even sinners.

The verse showing that Ram gave Lav and Kush the command to rule the mortal world appears as the sixteenth verse of the ninth canto of the Uttarkand in the Adhyatma Ramayan: _Prasthapayamasa cha tau Ramabhadrah kushilavau, ashtau rathasahasrani sahasram chaiva dantinam. ||5||_ (That night, having made this resolve, he sent Kush and Lav each to his own kingdom, giving each of them eight thousand chariots, one thousand elephants, and eight thousand horses.)

That is, before taking away everyone — Gandharvas and all — from Ayodhya, Ram first enthroned his two sons: he crowned Kush over the kingdom of Kosala and Lav over the region of North Kosala, handing separate kingdoms to the two brothers. Then Lord Ramchandra withdrew his divine play. Thus Ayodhya became desolate; no one remained there. Jivanji Maharaj came to this original Ayodhya and had darshan of all its sites — the site of Ramchandraji's palace, and the ground where Sitaji and Lakshman had dwelt. He saw the site of Bharatji's dwelling, bathed in the river Sarayu, and recited a sakhi.

_Main Ayodhyame Jivana, man mero Gokul manhi. Rishi patnisu kol hai, ve birad visrat nahi. ||6||_ (Meaning: Lord Ramchandra speaks to himself, saying: O Jivan, my mind is not truly attached to this play I am now enacting in Ayodhya; rather, my mind is fixed on the age to come, in which I am to take the Krishna avatar. I long for the moment when I shall assume the form of Krishna and fulfil the promise I gave to the sages' wives, letting them perform devotion to me — for, despite performing yajnas and other ritual acts, the sages themselves attained nothing, but their wives, through devotion, recognised Lord Ram and pleaded with him, "Grant us the opportunity to serve you." Ram promised he would grant them this opportunity at his birth as Krishna. It is in keeping with this episode that Jivanji Maharaj recites this sakhi at Ayodhya.)

Thus, staying in Ayodhya, Jivanji Maharaj remembers the life of Gokul; the memory of this leela of Shri Krishna comes back to him, and so he recites this sakhi. Our Jivanji Maharaj himself was one of the sixteen companions (sakhas) of Shri Krishna, and so it is only natural, and fitting to the place, that this memory should come to him here.
